title: Judges 12:8–15
context: Three minor judges follow Jephthah: Ibzan of Bethlehem, Elon the Zebulunite, and Abdon the Pirathonite. Each judged for some years and was buried in his hometown. Their notices mention large families, marriages outside the clan, and sons riding donkey colts, which suggest prosperity and standing. No battles are reported. It is uncertain whether Ibzan’s Bethlehem was the town in Judah or the one in Zebulun (Joshua 19:15). Both traditions read these brief records as signs of God’s continued care for Israel through ordinary leadership in quieter seasons. They also note that the book is moving toward greater disorder and the need for a faithful king.

verses.text: After him Ibzan of Bethlehem judged Israel.
verses.arminianNotes:
After Jephthah, Ibzan of Bethlehem judges Israel. A minor judge is introduced.

Arminian readers note that God continues to provide leadership for Israel, even after a turbulent period. Israel is not left without a judge after Jephthah’s troubled years.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that it is uncertain whether this Bethlehem is the town in Judah or the one in Zebulun (Joshua 19:15).

Both traditions treat the identification cautiously and see in Ibzan’s judgeship God’s ongoing care for his people.

verses.text: He had thirty sons. He sent his thirty daughters outside his clan, and he brought in thirty daughters from outside his clan for his sons. He judged Israel seven years.
verses.arminianNotes:
Ibzan had thirty sons and thirty daughters, sent his daughters outside his clan for marriage, and brought in wives from outside for his sons. He judged seven years.

Arminian readers note that the marriages may have built alliances and peace across clans.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the large family suggests prosperity and standing, perhaps a sign of God’s blessing in a quieter season.

Both traditions avoid overinterpreting the details and read the verse as a brief record of a stable leadership.

verses.text: Ibzan died, and was buried at Bethlehem.
verses.arminianNotes:
Ibzan dies and is buried at Bethlehem. His story is brief.

Arminian readers note that faithful leadership does not always produce dramatic stories; ordinary service also matters to God. Burial in his own town suggests a settled life ending in peace.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the burial notice marks the end of a life under God’s providence. Not every judge is remembered for battles.

Both traditions take encouragement that God values quiet faithfulness as well as heroic deeds.

verses.text: After him, Elon the Zebulunite judged Israel; and he judged Israel ten years.
verses.arminianNotes:
Elon the Zebulunite judges Israel ten years. Another minor judge follows.

Arminian readers note that God raises leaders from different tribes, showing that no tribe is excluded from his purposes. Zebulun, a northern tribe, now supplies Israel’s leader, and the calling of God is not confined to the prominent tribes.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that a decade of leadership without recorded crisis suggests a period of relative peace under God’s care, a mercy easily overlooked.

Both traditions read the verse as testimony to God’s continued provision for Israel.

verses.text: Elon the Zebulunite died, and was buried in Aijalon in the land of Zebulun.
verses.arminianNotes:
Elon dies and is buried in Aijalon in Zebulun. His name and his burial place are similar in Hebrew.

Arminian readers note that the record honors Elon’s service, even though little is known about him.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that this Aijalon in Zebulun is distinct from the better-known Aijalon in the south. God’s record includes the obscure.

Both traditions read the verse as a reminder that faithful service is remembered by God, even when history records little.

verses.text: After him, Abdon the son of Hillel the Pirathonite judged Israel.
verses.arminianNotes:
Abdon son of Hillel the Pirathonite judges Israel. A third minor judge appears.

Arminian readers note that God continues to raise leaders, showing his patience with a people often unfaithful. Each new judge is a fresh sign that God has not abandoned Israel.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Pirathon is later named as the hometown of one of David’s mighty men (2 Samuel 23:30). God’s providence links generations.

Both traditions read the verse as part of the record of God’s faithful provision.

verses.text: He had forty sons and thirty sons’ sons who rode on seventy donkey colts. He judged Israel eight years.
verses.arminianNotes:
Abdon had forty sons and thirty grandsons who rode on seventy donkey colts, and he judged eight years. Riding donkeys suggests status.

Arminian readers note that the description resembles that of Jair (10:4), a sign of wealth and standing.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the prosperity of these judges may reflect God’s blessing, though some interpreters see in it a hint of growing royal-style privilege.

Both traditions hold the meaning cautiously and avoid overreading the details.

verses.text: Abdon the son of Hillel the Pirathonite died, and was buried in Pirathon in the land of Ephraim, in the hill country of the Amalekites.
verses.arminianNotes:
Abdon dies and is buried in Pirathon in Ephraim, in the hill country of the Amalekites. The minor judges’ section ends.

Arminian readers note that the reference to the Amalekites is unusual and may reflect an earlier history of the region.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that interpreters differ on the meaning of the phrase, and it remains uncertain.

Both traditions read the close of this section as a pause before the story of Samson, where Israel’s condition will grow darker and the need for a faithful deliverer will become clearer.
